blocks.x: This is over at Joe Thomas' home at St. Anne, right near Galvez. And the date is September 29, 1960. This is Bill Russell and Ralph Collins is here interviewing Mr. Thomas here. If you could give us your name, your full name to start.
Yes, I'm Joseph William Thomas.
Can you tell us just when you were born?
Yes, December the 3rd, 1902.
You're about 53 years old.
Well, a little old, a little more than that, 57.
Yeah, 57.
Oh, sure, 57.
Yes.
I took out five.
Yeah, it'll be 58 December the 3rd coming.
Did your parents play any musical instruments? Your father, mother?
No, no, never did. All these kind of instruments they played, like this broom. You know, my dad used to put that broom on his tongue and make bass with that. I've seen Slow Greg do that.
Yeah, that's right.
It's got a good tone on it. My mother, she'd be singing and then my uncle, he'd take a comb and put the silver paper on it and play music like that.
Wait a minute, what's that with the broom, how they do that?

Oh, put your thumb on the table and a broomstick. Put a little rosin on that broomstick and just pull that stick over the thumb and it'd make a sound like a bass. The vibration from the table and that stick, it'd be a real bass violin.
Doesn't wear your thumb out?
Well, no. Daddy played that thing. Long time he did that.
Once I saw Slow Greg, he held his hand on the door, on a big door that would vibrate. Yes.

Sounds like a bass. It was. You see that? Yeah, well, there's so many ways you could do them things. I mean, I used to get some music out of it too. Yeah, I know. Yeah, we had a lot of singers in our family too. My sister sings, my dad and my mother, they all used to sing. Oh, yeah. I have a cousin, Pauline, she sings too.
What part of town were you born in, right here in New Orleans?
Yes, I was born on Taunty between Domaine and St. Anne, right across from the Taunty Social and Pleasure Club.
Not far from here then?
Not far.
You lived all your life in this neighborhood?

Well, when I got married, I got married on Iberville Street while I stayed up there quite a while. I moved up on Gravy and Durbin and I stayed up there about 18 years. But I'm back down in my old neighborhood where I was born and raised in the same neighborhood.
Have any brothers or sisters that learned music?
Well, one brother, he was trying to learn, but he had the wrong kind of instrument. He had a C melody saxophone and it didn't go so good with it. Well, he didn't try since that.
Nowadays, nobody plays that C melody anymore. No, no one.
I never heard of anyone playing it. See, it goes with a church organ, I think. Yeah. Yes. But otherwise, it's not good for, you know, for orchestra. Yes.
Those family get-togethers, you say, when your father played with the broom there. What kind of songs did you play here? Can you remember any of the names of the tunes or anything?

Well, let me see. I could, if I could think. Well, like, you know, Mr. Moon, Bright and Silver, Silvery Moon. Oh, yeah. That's a green shining light on me. Well, that's one of them. Yeah. And, uh, it was such old numbers, I can't quite remember them right off hand.
But they'd be popular tunes that you'd, uh, try?

Well, they were. I've heard them played lately, the numbers that my dad and mother and them used to sing and play. Yeah, they used to play them lately. Did they sing and play any hymns in your home? Well, no, it wasn't much, not much on hymns. You see, uh, no, they didn't play with the, you know, everybody was drinking, so I guess they didn't want to mix no hymns with liquor. Drinking and talking and laughing and then playing these tunes.

That time I heard Slowdrag, his wife had a little quartet there. They were playing some hymns, you know, she sings and plays in a church. Yeah. They were, they were using all hymns that night that I heard them. Uh-huh. And Slowdrag was using the broom. I just wondered if they might have had that in your home, too.

Yeah, no, they used to play it down by the old mill stream, I remember that. Yeah. And, oh, quite a few numbers, but, you know, it'd take time for them to come to it, you know. Oh, yeah. Sure. But, uh, they used to make good music with that kind of singing and that stick, or that broomstick for the bass.
And you say they had a comb and paper? Who?

What else did they play? Yeah, a soap paper and a comb. And then, at the time, they used to have some things called a gazoot. Oh, yeah. They'd have soap paper and a little tin horn. Yeah, I had one of those. Yeah, they used to play that, too. And I mean, we used to have some fun with those things. I'd be listening at them, you know, trying to sing with them, because I was a small kid then, you know. Right. Just trying to sing with them, and I used to enjoy that. We used to have a lot of fun. Yeah. I mean, wonderful time. And so, I can't remember the other numbers right now. Yeah, sure.
About that time when you were just a young fellow there, did you ever follow any parades at all at that time?

No, I did not. My power was very strict on me. They wouldn't let us go out the neighborhood. And then, nine o'clock at night, he'd blow that whistle, put his finger between his teeth and blow that whistle. He'd have to get on in and go to bed. And during the daytime, well, I'd either be at school or come from school right at the house. And so, I never had a chance to file in bands at my, you know, when I was small.
Did you hear any bands go by at all?

Well, yes, I remember, used to have parades pass all these streets sometimes, you know. Or, they were on Claiborne where my mother's, I tell you when we were small, I tell you what would happen. My grandmother would bring us on Canal Street to see the carnival parades. Yeah, and then, I remember her bringing us on Claiborne Street to see a group called the Hobgoblins. I've heard of them, yeah. The Hobgoblins. And them old time musicians was playing for them Hobgoblins. I think Larry Barbrand's dad was one of the musicians playing in that band at that time, yes. They used to be the Hobgoblins, a parade, and they'd be dressed with different things on their head, you know, like ghosts or something. Yes, I mean, I used to go on Claiborne Street and see that. Well, my grandmother, my mother always be with my parents though. I never could get up there by myself. No, no, no. No. But after I've grown some, then I was able to get around myself when I got much older, see, I guess we were in my late twenties maybe.
Do you remember any of the early dance bands that you hear when you were younger? Like on a wagon or anything, advertising maybe?

Yes, I remember Kid Punch, Kid René, Buddy Petit, Chris Kelly. I remember all of them. Right there on Orleans, they used to have a, it was an open lot, but they had built a platform on Orleans and White. That was years ago. And Kid Punch Band used to play back there. For dancing? Yes, uh-huh. Yeah, they used to have some fun. Is that a little park or not? But I was too, you know, to be going in, so all I'd do is stand on our side and listen. I had them play, you know, stand by the fence and get them. That would be like an open lot, you said. It was an open lot, but they had a pavilion built in the place, you know. Oh, so many feet off the ground. And the people would dance, the band would play, and the people would dance in there. I'd be out there listening to Adam and looking at them and having that fun. I remember it was Kid Punch playing there then.
How did that music in those days compare with the music that you hear now? Was it very similar or pretty much the same or different?

Well, it was, let me see, let me see. It was a little different in a way, but I tell you bands like Rene Punch, Buddy Petit, while they were playing the music almost similar to what we're playing now. Oh yeah. Yes. And sometime it'll be better. Yeah. Because them boys, they just was gifted and they really knew what they were doing. They just was gifted. I don't think they knew a bit of music. If they did, I didn't know anything about it. They had a good head for it. You see. Yeah. When did you start to learn and study music? Oh, well, I'll tell you when I first began music in 1923. I was a white gentleman living across from the Arcade Theater. So, someone told me he had a clarinet for sale. So, they knew I wanted to, you know, I used to try to beat the drum, I used to sing. They knew I would, had liked music. So, they told me about this gentleman. So, I went to see him about it. So, he said, yeah, he was selling me the clarinet. He wanted $5 for it. He said, he let me have it for $5. And so, guess how I got the money? I had a Christmas saving that year. The bank right there on Sedan and Cleveland. It used to be a bank there. And I saved up that whole year. And guess how much it was that I saved? $5 that whole year. Christmas saving. So, I taken that $5 check and brought it right to him and got this client. It was an Albert system. Albert system. Yeah, B-flat clarinet. And so, from that I start making noise around the house, trying to learn how to blow it. My mother would run out with all that noise. And, Thomas, get out of here. She used to call me Brother. My nickname was Brother. I said, Brother, get out of here with all that noise. I'd go out in the backyard. We had a large backyard. I'd go in the yard and try to blow it again. So, finally I find myself playing Hum, Sweet Hum, Nearer, My God, The D. And a few other numbers like that. So, the boy said, Brother, why don't you go take some lessons? Say, you did all that much by yourself. You take a lesson, you know, give you more ideas. So, I decided to take a lesson. So, I went to Chalini. Old man Chalini. He was living on St. Claude, between Domaine and St. Philip. I went there and he started giving me lessons. A, B, C, D, R, A, Mi, Fa, Son, that's it. About how old were you then? Well, it was in 24 then. 1924. You see? So, that make I was about... 22 years old. 23 years old. That's it. Yes. I was about 23 years old. And, so I got to... Did he use a book?
How did he teach you? I wondered what kind of...

He teach me out of a music book. A real music book. Not the regular music book then. But, he was teaching me out of a book he had around then. So, after I got to making my scales so good, so he recommended me to get a clarinet book. Oto Lange clarinet book. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. So, gee, I was playing up some music in that clarinet book. The scales, you know, chromatic scales, ascending and descending. I was doing all that. And then, I used to play in a brass band with him. He had a brass band. He had a son who used to lead the band. And Sean Lee always was there, giving us ideas how to play. We used to rehearse at the... Scent of Sinners. Yeah. On Demain Street. Scent of Sinners Club. Yeah.
Uh-huh. We used to rehearse there.
And, so... Is that a dance band or a brass band? It was a brass band. Uh-huh. Yes.
All, gee, about four or five clarinets. I had an uncle who was playing in that band then, too.

Uh, Wellington Knox. Yeah. He gave up the clarinet. And then, quite a few... Is he still living? Yeah, he's still living. Yes. Is he any relation to Mr. Knox who plays drum in the Young Tuxedo band with Casabin? Uh, no. I don't think there's any relation, no. Uh, I don't think there's any relation, no. Uh, I don't... Emile Knox.
Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. Uh, I don't think there's any relation.
But, uh, he used to play clarinet with...
Is he still living? Yeah, he's still living, yes. Is he in any relation with Mr. Knox who plays drum in the Young Tuxedo band with Kazimier?

No, I don't think they're in any relation, no. I don't believe. Emil Knox. Yeah, I know you're talking about he played with John Kazimier. I don't think they're in any relation. But he used to play clientele, Shalini was teaching him too, but he gave it up. And quite a few boys that I remember when I started gave it up. How often did you take a lesson? Once a week or more often? Oh, about once a week I was gone. See, about once a week.
How long did the lesson last?
Well, the lesson lasted about a half an hour or so.
Do you remember what he charged you in those days for lessons?

Yeah, 25 cents. 25 cents, that's what I was paying. And if I'm not mistaken, it went up just a little bit. Might have only 50 cents after it. That's 25 cents a lesson. Was he a very strict teacher or how did he do? Oh, he was very strict. Yeah.
Yeah, well he'd slap you, you know, make the wrong note. Wait a while, you're making the wrong note. He would slap you, yeah. He was very strict. Did he ever play? But he was good though.
Did he ever play anything with you on any instrument?

Well he tried but the only thing he could play was the trumpet and he didn't do such a good job because at the time he was losing his teeth and more wind would come from the side of the mouth than through the instrument. Yeah, he tried to play, to show you what he wants you to make, but he wasn't so good at it. But he was really good at teaching. Good musician now. Yeah, I mean, and so he taught me good. So he had me reading music good. I was really reading from a little red book, a little red book they used to call it.
The ragdine pieces?
Yeah, some kind of book for the brass bands, you know, it would be a red book. Yeah, we used to play all the numbers out of that book, you know, parades and everything. But all that got away from it.
How long did you take lessons from him about?
About, I'd say a year or a year or so, yes.
Well, the clarinet you got was the Albert system, was it?
It was an Albert, yes. It was an Albert system. That's all new then, you know.
A 15 key Albert? Yeah, 15 keys, yes.

Uh-huh. Yeah, well, that's what I had when I bought from this gentleman, the month of December, when I bought it from him. It was a 15 key Albert. I kept it a pretty good while. And somehow or another, I don't know what happened, if I lost it, I can't remember. But John Lewis, while playing, you know, John Lewis loaned me a clarinet once. A silver clarinet. Oh, yeah. And I played that thing, I mean, for a good while. And so, I'm finished telling you, when I got to playing that music good, you know, and well, I used to be at the house reading different music and trying to learn more and more. Well, it's a boy named Gilbert Young, I think you all know him, who played trumpet. Well, he and I used to rehearse, and a few other boys, I can't remember the names, used to rehearse on all these near Russia players, different numbers. And while we picked up this number, sophisticated lady, and we tried to play that, that was a headache, trying to read that number. I mean, never could get that number straight. But then I went, while, during this, uh, that's where I had a boy named Gerald Kendrick. Uh, he said, brother, he said, uh, you play good enough, would like to be playing in a band. I said, yeah, but, I said, but, uh, I don't know, you all play by music? He said, no, we play by air. I said, okay, so I went to start playing music, jobs with him, you know, and called us a riffing. What did he play?
Kendrick?
Kendrick, Gerald Kendrick, uh, trumpet player. Yeah. And, uh, I haven't seen that boy for years now.
Remember anybody else in the band? You have a trombone, bass, guitar?

Well, uh, boy, uh, boy named, uh, played trombone. Oh, gee, I, I can't call his name either. He doesn't play now anymore. Nobody we know. No, no, he don't play now. Uh, cause Buster played with the band at one time for a while. Mr. Moore? Yes, uh-huh. He played with the band. But this boy I'm trying to call, I can't recall his name now. And I think George Young played with, with this band when I first started playing. And you know the only thing I got to playing by air with the band and all the music I'd like, just went away. Didn't, didn't bother with it anymore? No, I didn't bother with it. It got away from you? It got away from you. Yeah. That's the truth. That's right, it does, doesn't it? It got away from me. I tell them, boy, how much I used to read. A lot of them knew it. Yeah. A lot of them knew how I could read all that music, but now I can't really know it, big as the customer. And so it just really-
Well, if you put your mind to it and had to do it, it'd come back to you.
Well, yeah, well, a late little band been rehearsing and so they expect to learn a lot of numbers, you know, by music. And so I've been getting myself brushed up on it. I noticed it up myself.
If you start trying to play things without music, it's pretty soon you can't play them when you get back to the music. That's right.

Well, then I finished playing with Gerald Kendrick, well, then I started playing with other groups. Well, and those years ago I even played with Jack Carey at Brown's Velvet Ice Cream Place. And I made four dollars that night. Gee, I thought I made big money.
What was that, the advertised for the ice cream or what?
No, he was playing for a dance like, a party like, inside of Brown's Velvet Plant on Brown's Street. He was playing for a dance, a party there had put on.
Yeah.

Then I played with Kid René years ago. I played with John Lewis, played with John Lewis, a ticket seat. So Kid René got me to play with him. Well, I played a few jobs with Chris Kelly. Yeah, I played a few jobs at the Corborator Hall, the Economy Hall. Yeah, I played with them old guys. And I really enjoyed playing with them. I got a lot of experience, you see. And Kid Thomas, he came from over the river once and played back on St. Peter's Street, it was like a lumber yard but they cleaned it up and made a dance place out of it. Well I went over there and played with him, the Kid Thomas band. Well he was hot stuff then. Every time I was surprised they'd say, Kid Thomas coming over. He had about the best band here. Yeah, he still got a good band. Yeah, he still got a pretty good band, yeah. Kid Thomas was good. And I played with him over the river quite a few times, yes. And, well anyhow.
Can you tell us any more about Chris Kelly, how he sounded? I never got to hear him.

Well I tell you, Chris Kelly sounded good. Chris Kelly was a great musician. And, and I'm talking about the blues. Nobody beat him playing blues. I heard he was a good blues player. Yes, and he put that wow wow mute, that stop or whatever you know. Rubber plunger thing. Yeah, plunger. I mean get the wow wow and then, boy I say, you really went over for that. Went over big. Yeah, Chris Kelly was a great musician. Yeah, when I think about this time, Chris Kelly, Buddy PT, Jack Carey, Kid Punch. I think them boys played some music in them days. How did Punch sound then?
I've only heard him in the last few years. Who?
Punch. Oh gee, Punch could make more on the trumpet than I could make on the clarinet. Really?
A lot of fast notes and all that?

Yeah, he was fast, yes. Punch could variate that trumpet. I never saw a man variate the trumpet that much like Punch used to do it. And I mean some wonderful notes he'd come out that horn, you know, and he'd go. He'd do some wonderful variation. He'd behead me skint on the clarinet at the time. I couldn't make that much of him up. Punch really was good.
He didn't play a lot of high notes around him, did he, at that time? Who? Punch. He didn't do it.
No, not, no. Very few high notes he would make. All in the staff. All in the staff. Yeah, but he'd be variating, I mean, on that trumpet.
They say Buddy Petit could do a lot of that stuff. Was he like that?

Yeah, Buddy Petit too. Yeah, he was. Yeah, he was like that. Well, Kid René, Kid René could variate a lot too. I'll tell you, they were real good musicians. Those street boys, you know, that I can remember now, they were street. They were really good. They knew what they were doing and they would do it. They'd look like they'd do it better and better each time they would come out. They'd play better and better. I tell you, they really was a wonderful group to play with. And I enjoyed playing with them because it gave me a lot of experience. That's why now I could play so many of those numbers that they played years ago. And then listening at Louis Armstrong records too, it caused me to be able to play it a lot of numbers. Like the Dipper Martin or the Clarinet part or the Marshall Bobcats. I got that listening at Orvin Frazola. Yeah, listening at him. And then quite a few numbers I'll make parts for, you know, listening at these fellas. Well, they gave me an idea of just how to make it and what to make.
One time I wanted to ask you, brother, it was, well first I wanted to ask you, how long have you had your nickname Brother Cullenbrack?
Well, I'll tell you, that name came when I was going to school. Oh yeah. My mother used to give me cornbread to take to school with me.
Ever since then? Ever since then.
Them boys saw that cornbread and they've been calling me cornbread ever since.
But before that it was just brother, was it?

Brother, yes. That's all, just brother. Brother William. We had a nickname, uh, nickname William. Well that's my middle name, William. But they used to call my daddy William, so they'd call me brother William. And, with that cornbread, the game was from my school days and it's been still ever since.
Well, I wonder to ask you, when did you switch to this band system, Cullen actually got down?
Well, that was when I was playing at the H and J Tavern. Now, it was during the war, World War II I believe.
I think I first heard you, I was staying with George Lewis one summer for about a month and he said go over there and hear Brother Cullenbrack, I think he called you. Yeah.
At that time. Uh, where I was then.
And that's where, it was on, um, that was 1943. Yeah. Is that the place on, um, St. Bernard? St. Bernard, yeah. Yeah, the H and J Tavern. The H and J Tavern.

Yeah, that's it. That's the place. Well, I bought this clarinet for my son. So, he got to learn a little bit of horn at these. Learned pretty good, you know. And so he went to California with the horn. And then he came back again. And so, I noticed he wasn't bothering with it. I said, well, George, you know, you're not going to play the clarinet? He said, Dad, I don't care to play the horn. I said, well, no. I said, no. I said, well, I can't let it lay here and go to waste. So, I used to take that horn and my albert system to H and J on the job. I tried to play a number with the BAM system and I couldn't. I put it down and pick up the albert. So, finally, I got to learn the BAM system little by little. And now, I can't play the albert no more.
Oh, yeah, you got to work in the albert now.
Got to work in the albert.
Anybody else show you how the fingering was different on it? Or you worked it out yourself?

I worked it out myself, yeah. Worked it out yourself. Yeah, just felt my way myself because there wasn't no clarinet player. No, only anybody plays. No, and so, I just worked it out myself. Just kept feeling my way and finally got the BAM system to work in. Now, since that, I tried to play albert. And so, I got a different fingering, you know.
You noticed much difference in the tone. Is there any difference in the sound of it, do you think, aside from the fingering?
I didn't tell you it should. I couldn't, I swear I'd notice any difference in a thing like that.
But if it's easier to play louder or a bigger tone on the albert or on the BAM, which blows easier?
I think it's easier to play louder and bigger tone. Because you have much more keys to make some different notes, I think. That, that's a, might be a different on that.
It's easier to, it can get the blow bigger tone on the BAM.

On the BAM system, yes, yes. It's easier to get the bigger tone out of it. Now, another thing to help you to make a bigger tone. Me, I've been using the stiff reed, a tree in the head. And I could play it very loud, because sometimes the boys tell me, I said, brother you're too loud. Well, I have a strong lip. You see, I've been playing without my teeth. Yeah, I noticed you.
I was going to say you've played without your teeth, don't you?

For quite a while. And now, it's another thing I've got to start learning how to play with these teeth in my mouth. Yeah. I tell me, John Lewis, the man, he got his teeth in. Yeah. I can't understand, but I can't do it myself. Yeah, it takes quite a while, I think.
I tried.
You can take one set out and let the other set in. I may got a little bit with it, you know, but it didn't sound too good.
That's what I was going to ask you, brother. When you switched clarinets, did you have to switch mouthpieces, or did you just use the mouthpiece that came on it?
The mouthpiece that came on the BAM system, I used it. Do you find any difference in the blowing?
Did you have to blow harder or less hard or anything like that?
No, the blow is softer because I noticed when I blew hard, it would make false noise. Yeah, yeah. It would make a plain sound. I've noticed that myself.
That's why I asked you that because it seems like in a BAM system, you shouldn't blow quite so hard. You don't have to blow quite so hard. You don't have to blow quite so hard.
You don't have to blow quite so hard. I noticed that.

that's the truth because uh you do it squeaks when you blow too hard. I found that out and then being a new instrument too that's another thing it was newer than the old Albert I'd been playing for years you see so that made a difference too. Being new it was much easier so I was forced to blow softer to get a tone out of it otherwise it would squeak. Were you still playing the Silver Albert of George Laws at that time? No, was I still playing? Oh no I gave it back to George and after keeping it maybe a month or two months. Oh I see. Yeah and since I bought that five dollar clarinet I have owned about
six seven clarinets. Oh yeah. Yes. But this uh band that you're playing is that still the one you bought for your son?

Yes the same one. The same one. Yes. Oh that sounds good. Yeah. Uh uh but since that I bought another band system since that though. Oh yeah? Yeah well I played both of them now. Oh I see you take two out now. Two out yeah well I might leave one home for two three months play the other one and then I'll play the one I bought for my son. The last one I bought was from Peterson. Any particular make that
you like on it or? Uh I mean uh. Is it a brand like is it a Selmer or a Conor? Well I'll tell you I'd rather

have Selmer. I expect to buy a Selmer by the beginning of next year. Yeah. Selmer kind of yes. Uh but this was a region where I bought during the war for my son and for from Peterson it was uh oh I can't call the name right now. But uh I really would like to get me a Selmer clarinet because all the boys in the band say they're always bragging about the Selmer. It's the best and so I'd like to get one and you know what I expect to get to? A tenor sax. Oh yeah. And the fella said brother good good as clarinet you could play it. So you'd raise sand on a tenor sax. Did you ever play sax any of us? No never did. Never did.
I don't know I've heard people say if you play too much sax you'll lose your lip for your clarinet.

You'll lose your lip for your clarinet, yes. Well that's what I could be afraid of. Yeah you don't want to do that. No I sure wouldn't want to do that because uh clarinet is the thing that kept me going all these years years. Of course one time ago I had to count on these smaller bands but since uh Dixieland came and swing well I'm running much more.

I don't know. He can't. Well he could still play now. He plays all right now but I guess not as well as it used to. Not as well as it used to. Um yeah and so. I was going to say some people like the Leblanc clarinet. Some people think they're the best nowadays. They're made in France but they're put together over in this country.

Oh really? Leblanc. I have a Leblanc case but but it's not a Leblanc clarinet. I can't call the name of that horn. I bought from Peterson. Uh it's a French horn though. It's French? Yeah it's a French horn. Yeah like a buffet. It's a French horn. It's a French horn. It's a French horn. It's a French horn. It's a French horn. It might come to the later. Yeah. I can't think of the name of it but it seems to be a pretty good horn. Uh what the boy said is well you see it sounds no I'll tell you I bought a horn through Larry Barberan from a boy that was going to this Grunwald school of music. Yeah he you know got tired of the horn. He didn't care to play anymore and so I bought the horn through Larry Barberan I think for about 40 or 50 dollars I think. A nice clarinet. I can't remember the name of it either.

Well I was going to ask who were some of the clarinetists that you liked when you were young and getting started. You mentioned all those trumpet players like Punch and Kid Rene. Who were some of the better clarinetists when you were young learning that you liked to hear?

Well I'll tell you I used to be tickled to death to hear Georgia Barrett. Oh yeah. I mean Georgia Barrett yeah. He was my favorite. Yeah. I never got to know him. You never got to know him? No? No. No he died years ago. Kid Howard was playing with him or he was playing with Kid Howard.

No Lee Collins used to talk to me about him. He'd leave once. Lee Collins had me to go down. I met his widow. You met his widow? I saw a picture of him. She was living up on Perdido Street. All that's torn down. I don't know where she is now.
No Miss Rose or Daisy I think the name is.
I think that's it.
Yeah. I don't know where she moved either because I was surprised when I went around there saw all that torn down.
Yeah it's all torn down.
So I guess maybe inquiring in the neighborhood I might could find out where she lived.

Most of the time, we, the trumpet and the clarinet would be on one side, the drum would be on the other, and the banjo may be next to the drum. Uh-huh. But the trombone and bass would usually be in the rear, because a lot of times the truck had a top on it, and so the bass player, you either have to lay bass down and play it, or get to the rear of the truck, so you could hold it straight up.
Yes, that's right.

Oh, we experienced one of the, was, we always experienced one of the, uh, advertising, uptown somewhere, I can't remember the street, you know, I can't remember what bass player it was, but we were just a plane. And so, when the band stopped playing, well, we called, so we've gone to another corner. There was a tree hanging low, a tree branch. That bass got hooked to that tree branch, there go the bass, and the bass player, he hung on to his bass. Oh, my God. Hanging on that tree, you know, had to go help him down. And if you happen to run across some of the boys, they might could tell you who it was, but I can't remember who it was, but that really happened. That tree grabbed that bass and pulled it off the truck, and the bass player with it. I know it wasn't Sidney Brown, because Sidney Brown was too big. He couldn't hold it. I just couldn't. It was a small bass player, I can't remember. Somebody may tell you about it. That was the worst experience I ever witnessed. Oh, I thought we'd have had some trouble with the experience. Because one time I used to travel, I was traveling with a band, and a bass player, well, that was Frank Mills then. A fella called J.C. I used to travel with, I forget his whole name. Well, we were going somewhere through Mississippi. We had to pass a narrow bridge. One caught coming this way, one going that way. And the bass, you used to have to always keep the bass on the side, especially the one you wasn't going for. Well, that, all of you passed too close to that bridge railing and just towed that bass to pieces. I mean, Frank Mills said, oh, look what done happened to my bass. He was some downhearted. Yeah, the bass just torn up, you know, by passing close to the railing. Well, the fella couldn't do no better because another call was coming. It was an alley bridge. And so that, that bust up the, of Frank Mills bass and he was sure downhearted. So, while, when we got to this town where we were going, looking up to get another bass. The fella out there had a bass, we used it, you know, while we was out there. But that was something. And now, talking about the different bands I played with, well, I used to play with a band called the Yo-Yo Boys. No, well, I'll tell you who that was. Andrew Jefferson, Joe Goods. Joe Goods used to play, it was a wonderful banjo player when he gave it up because his daddy had a big band. Have a big dredge business. They lived on Ivyville Street. So, doing so much business, so he gave up the banjo. Now, his name was Joe Goods. And then we had a boy named Red, he used to play the gazoot, Lil Red they called him. And Brady, he, no, Brady wasn't with us then because Andrew Jepson was with us. And Stackely played piano. You know Stackely? I've heard of him, don't know anything about him. No, no.
Is that the same color they made the blues up about?
No, no, it's not.

Somebody else, yeah. But his name was really Stagley. It's a wonder he didn't make up this number, but they beat him. Somebody beat him to it. They used to call him Stagley. His name is Lawrence Tunnage. Put it back down on the feet near broad. Does that mean anything, that name, Stagley? Or is it just a name? Well, not that I know of. No. I don't know who it means anything, but just a name. That's all I could.
We're going to say, when was the last time you played in that Buddhist man on that track? Oh, gee. It's been quite a while now. I don't know. I was wondering what happened.

Because I used to play every year. Somebody had to play on the track, advertisement, you know. But the last time, yes, I had to meet some boys. Yeah, I played with Peter Williams. Played with the advertisement. Peter Williams. I think this was for a picnic that was going on the next Sunday. Peter Williams. Peter Williams. Peter Williams. And who else he had playing with him? And then I would play that advertisement all uptown. We left around Jackson Avenue and Galveston. And we went all over uptown. We didn't come down this way. Is that since the war? Yes, since the war. And we played all over, advertising for this picnic that was going on the next Sunday. Yeah. Yeah. That's unusual because most of the time when the band advertised on a truck or something. It's for a dance that night. Yeah. I've seen that. Yeah. But this was a picnic for the next Sunday. And we were advertising the Sunday before. Yeah. Trying to get up some customers. Yeah. And so. Well, that's about the last one I remember playing. You don't remember what year that would be. You don't remember what year that would be. I know it was in the 50s. She was 61 now. I would say about 52 or 53 because it was better than seven, eight years ago. Yeah. I remember one about 1952 about the last I saw advertising a dance that night. Yeah. For a long party or something. The bands really don't have them no more do they? No, I guess not much. Yeah, because I really don't run across. I don't hear nobody playing any. Now the only thing I've seen lately was a band on the truck. Not Carnival Pass but Carnival Before That. What was that Carnival? When it's Milton and them. Playing on the neutral ground in the truck. But they wasn't going the way. They just was in that one place. You know. Playing. Playing music. stuff I was about to go get my clarinet, but it was so late when I got around here because our job ran late that day. So I got to get my horn while he was breaking up. Otherwise I would sit in with him too. Yeah, I really had a wonderful time at that carnival on that corner. Everybody drinking their beers, canned beers and all, and standing around the truck listening to music. And then the Zulus passing right after that.
I see quite a few on the carnival day that have bands on the parade. Not so many the last carnival or last year or two, but before that I've had quite a few.
Yeah, quite a few.
So we're talking about Mardi Gras. Where's the best place and what's the best time to find the Indians?

The best place is on Corn Eye Street. Corn Eye and Gavis or Corn Eye and Johnson, Corn Eye and Nero. Well, there's one group that meets around there every year. I beat up the Yallapocahunters, they call them. Yeah, you'll find them.
What time was the best time?

Well, they get dressed early. You see them getting together around 8 o'clock in the morning. Oh, yes. 8 o'clock in the morning. Some of them pass here going up there. You know, they live all over the city. So they pass through here going to Corn Eye and Johnson or Corn Eye and Nero. Either one of them.
I'll go around there next morning.
Yes, I'd like to see. Three or four years ago I saw some of them over that way. Yes.
Uh-huh.
Usually, I think I usually get around there too late in the day. Probably later in the afternoon when I get around there. And I guess by then the water was beginning to break up. Yes.
Well, uh.
You said in the morning would be the best time.

Yes, in the morning around 8 o'clock. They start getting together. Maybe sometime earlier. Or you see them getting together. Because it's the funny thing about carnival business. Them Indians, them boys, they'd be so anxious for that day to come. They might start dressing at night.
Did they ever have a band with them, the Indians, that you know of? Or what?
Any music?
Did they use any instruments or just sing with them?

No, they just sing. The only thing they ever have is tum tum, you know, tambourines. That's the only thing I've seen them with so far. They've beaten it against their hand and they make some music with those things. Yeah. Some fellas know how to beat those tambourines. They really mix a lot of music with them. Now, the only musical instrument I've ever seen them with on Mardi Gras did. Now, they might put on a dance, maybe that night, or either St. Joseph night, and you see them coming along at night with the red lantern or the white lantern, because the law allowed them to have a lantern, you see? Yeah. Ah, there's my sister coming in. Come right on. I heard him talking.
Yes.
My sister, Noella Mack. Mr. Bill Russell. Mr. Bill Russell.
Just interviewing Mr. Thomas at Tulane University. Mr. Bill.

Yes, she's another one who should have been in the limelight. You might have heard about the wonderful voice she has. Oh. She sings in the church choir. Everybody out there, even my piano player, Jeanette Kimball. Just Sunday, she was telling me. What church is the same? Mr. They have a lovely voice. It's St. Peter Claver Church. She sings in the choir there. Yeah. You got a Baptist church over there? Well, right here they have one in the block. Reverend Galveston.
Oh, Galveston. Yeah, Galveston and DuMaine. Right across from Joe Watkins. Oh, yeah.
Which church is your sister singing in that? St. Peter Claver.
The Catholic Church on the same front. What's the Catholic Church?
Yeah, between Prairie and Roman. She sings every Sunday, Tuesday night. I guess perhaps every night now because they're having a mission.
Well, anyhow. We might have a singing every night for benediction. Well, anyhow.

I'll finish talking like you were asking me to ask you to do it. What church is your sister singing in that? What church is your sister singing in that? St. Peter Claver. The Catholic Church on the same front. What's the Catholic Church? Yeah, between Prairie and Roman. She sings there every Sunday, Tuesday night. I guess perhaps every night now because they're having a mission. So, you might have a singing every night for benediction. Well, anyhow. I'll finish talking like you were asking me if I did have anybody in my family that played instruments. Well, like I told you, not that I know of, but they're always musically inclined. Yes. Even I have a cousin. I have a cousin. She's a wonderful songster. She just sings around the house. She sings at little parties.
Did we ask if you ever tried to play anything else besides clarinet, the instrument when you were young? Yes. Or?

Yes. A trombone. Well, I tell you, though, I was going to buy this trombone, but this fellow, I don't know how much he wanted for it, but I think he wanted a little too much. Before I thought about the clarinet, I guess I would have been a trombone player. Yeah. Now, you know what? I really should have been a piano player. You like that? I've been banging on the piano since I was very small, but the only thing I could play the numbers, but I don't have no bass and very little treble. You know, just play a straight lead. But I thought, sure, I would have been a piano player, but I just didn't go at it right. But the clarinet, you could make music with one note at a time. Well, I guess that's how I learned that. I'm going taking lessons. That gave me more ideas.
Did you say that you'd done a little drumming before you took out the clarinet today? A little what? Did you say you'd done some drumming or something?

No, no, no. I didn't do no drumming, no. Well, you might have heard me say I used to beat drum on a soapbox. You might have heard me say, yeah. Yeah. Because that's how the boys told me about getting an instrument because they thought I'd like music. Sure. I'm always beating on something with two sticks on a soapbox or on my mother's table until she'd run me out. Or you might take a spoon or a knife and play music with the spoons on the table. But after this gentleman mentioned about this clarinet for five hours, and I was getting five dollars from this bank here for a year of saving. So I bought a clarinet and that's what I've stuck to ever since.
You say you play a stick reed. Do you play a plastic reed or a wooden reed?

I never did play a plastic reed yet. The boys told me about it. Why don't I get a plastic reed? But I never did. Because sometimes they're alright and most of the time they're not. They cost more and all. They last longer. But I always feel like they may not blow right to me. Where there was reeds I wouldn't reed, cane reeds I'd buy. Well I figured if one don't do right I could chance to get another. They're just twenty and twenty-five cents. Sure.
A piece. Do you find that they last you quite a long time, cane reeds? How long?

Yes they last me quite a while. I could play, gee it was, sometime over a month with one cane reeds. It might crack on top but I trim it and gone again with it. Yeah I trim it you know, I take two pennies or two nickels and put it in between and take my cigarette and pass it on the edge and trim it all soft. I used to have a reed trimmer but I don't know what happened to it. You know I never got to buying another one but I used to have a reed cutter and it would cut the reed. But you know I keep forgetting to buy one so I got to use the home made.
And it works just as well.
It works just as well, yes. Then.
You use a penny, two pennies. Two pennies or two nickels.
Two nickels. And I put the end of the reed right between and I take my cigarette and just pass and I'll be blowing at the same time because if you don't blow right away it'll burn down.
Burn down.

Yes. And then I take a razor blade, sometimes it'll be too stiff after I trim it short. Take a razor blade and shave on top of the reed. That softens it up again. I could go another month with it. Play it another month. And so that's just the way I've been going along all the while with these cane reeds. I mostly buy them at Peterson on Broad Street. Sometimes I'll be in town and I'll buy some at Werlein or Grunewald. Because the clarinet I bought for my son, I bought it at Grunewald, this reed-er. The first damn system I ever bought. And Grunewald, I like to buy my reeds there too.
Did you use the same reeds, the same number or anything with your albeth or did you change?

With my albeth I think I used to use a limber, a more lighter reed. I used to use I believe two and two and a half. At the time I didn't know nothing about numbers, about reed numbers. You know there was a lot of things I didn't know about the clarinet. I was playing it, playing jobs, entertaining people. A lot of things I didn't know about until quite a few years after. Even putting that grease on the caulk, you know, in between the horn to, so the horn could come loose easily. Because one while I'm losing the caulk around my horn, so Peterson's the one told me, I said, brother you got any caulk grease? I said, what is that? So he showed me a little can and so he sold me the caulk grease. So I've been doing that ever since. But all before that I wouldn't use nothing like that and the caulk get dry and it's come right off. So I found out the caulk grease saved it. So since that I've been keeping up with caulk grease.
But you think you blew a softer reed with your Albert than you do with your Bear? Yes, I did, yes.
It was a softer reed because after, I believe Peterson was, when I started buying reeds from him, he asked me what number you want. I said number. I said number.

I said, did it go by number? He said, yeah. He said, you got one, one and a half, two. He said, one and a half is for beginners and youngsters, you know. And he said, two is for a person that's been playing or two and a half. Then he said, three and three and a half is for a person that likes a real stiff read. So I said, well, let's try a three and a half. And gee, I like it. I can make a better tone with that three and a half. As long as my lip is strong, they say I blow it out my teeth. And so I think as long as I have a strong lip, I get a better tone with a three and a half. And so that's what I've been using ever since. But I don't know. The last time I bought reads, Peterson claimed that I should get a two and a half because I'm older and I should use a soft read. I told him, okay. Did you see I went on a job with a two and a half? Didn't I? No.
Wouldn't make any difference? If you get a little older, wouldn't make sense?
Because I told him, I said, I think my lip is just as strong now as it was.
If you were going to drop a tall, you wouldn't, I don't think you should drop that much. I mean, if you dropped a tall, you only drop a half.
A half, man. I was good. A tree and a half should have been a tree, huh? Yeah.
I wouldn't think you'd need to drop unless you wanted to drop.

No, I don't think because, you see, if it's too stiff, you could always trim it with a razor blade. You know, there's always a way to make it soft if they're too hard. Yeah. So I said, well, from now on, I'll know better. And so I've been going along playing with a tree and a half and I've been doing all right. So when I go back there again and buy some more reeds, I'll be sure and see that it's tree and a half size. Because I think I do better with them kind than I do with any other.

Well, I was going to ask, in the Celestan's band, did you join him when he had more than one band? Sometime I heard he had a band that played at the paddock and then wanted to be out on the road sometime. Do you remember those days?

Yes, in a way, I did because we started, I started with him at, let me see, it was at the American Legion Hall on Ross Street. Well, Bill Matthews and them were supposed to play there with him. And it seemed like they already stayed at the paddock lounge and played. It was a count of a day. So Papa got all the, let me see, Saeed, Mercedes Fields in the little town. And Harrison Burrett, myself. And Eddie Pearson, yeah, to come play, to play at the American Legion Hall. So, so we played there. I know there was a big confusion in the body. That's when Papa fell out with them, when he fell out with Papa. So, and so, and then on, well, Papa didn't bother with him for a while. Then finally he went and stopped playing at the paddock lounge. He brought this other band to the paddock lounge. Yeah. Eddie Pearson and then Paul Barnes was playing clarinet. Well, I was with the band and Paul Barnes and myself, two clarineters, where Paul Barnes could play sax to. Well, Papa started playing at the paddock lounge. Well, that kind of shut me out. He was playing every night. And Paul Barnes never once said, well, let brother play one night. Yeah, so I just made myself satisfied until Papa got out the paddock lounge. We started playing jobs, different spots. And Paul Barnes went to California. Well, that made me be the regular clarinet player. So he quit bottom with Bill Matthews and Piku and all of, what you call them, Octave Cards. Yeah. Yeah, that's when the band got away from one of them. Yeah, I remember. Yeah, and so he just decided to call it Quits. But they played on Bourbon Street quite a long time. Yeah, probably had a wonderful, wonderful group up there. But he was both bands. He was doing all right. But he just learned things. Had a little falling out. So let me, let me call it. Papa went, went to himself, you know, got up another band. He was going for himself and let them stay where they were. I mean, we went to town for a good while. You know, while Papa was, uh, in the band. I mean, while he was living, did a lot of good.
Were you there with the band when Shatz played for the South Stand Kid Shatz?

No, I wasn't. No, I wasn't with the band then. No, I heard about Shatz playing with the band. And, uh, I think there was one Papa had the big band. That was way back, I think. Yeah. They played at the Pelican. No, it was about 1946. They played with the big band.
Yeah, they got the Pelican. He had a big orchestra then.

Yeah. And even a guy called, uh, I can't call it even in, I just got one called, a little trumpet player. He was good. Well, he was playing with Papa then. And, uh, just one of them things, uh, after that big band broke up, well, Papa had given up music for a while. He had given up music for a while. And I, once he made a comeback, cause he went to work at the shipyard. That's when he got hurt. Yeah, broke his leg. Broke his leg. That's right. And so, doing all right. Until then, and he'd give it up for a while and finally somebody went and seek him up. Yeah.
He tried to come back.
Yeah, made a comeback. I mean, a great comeback.
This reel is just about over, I guess. Yes. If you can call it.
Well, I think, that's all I can remember.
Well, I think you covered your life pretty well.
Yeah, thank you very much. You told us a lot of things about those old town bands too. Yeah, thank you very much.
I certainly enjoyed talking with you.
Yes, I really enjoyed.

segments.title: Opening, date and Thomas's birth
segments.summary: Russell announces the recording at Thomas's home on 29 September 1960; Thomas gives his name and birth date, December 3, 1902.

segments.title: Father's broom-bass and uncle's comb, a musical family
segments.summary: Neither parent played an instrument, but his father made bass sounds with a broomstick and rosin, his uncle played a comb, and the family sang.

segments.title: Born on Taunty Street; neighborhood and later homes
segments.summary: He was born near Domaine and St. Anne, moved after marriage to Iberville and Gravier/Durbin for 18 years, and is back in the old neighborhood.

segments.title: A brother's C-melody saxophone
segments.summary: One brother tried to learn music on a C-melody saxophone and gave up; Thomas says it suits a church organ, not an orchestra.

segments.title: Family singing, old tunes, comb-and-paper gazoo
segments.summary: He recalls songs like Silvery Moon sung and played at home with drinking and laughter, with no hymns, and the soap-paper gazoo he enjoyed as a small child.

segments.title: Strict upbringing; Hobgoblins parade
segments.summary: His strict father kept him home, so he could not follow bands as a boy; his grandmother took him to Canal Street carnival parades and the Hobgoblins on Claiborne.

segments.title: Early dance bands: Kid Punch's platform at Orleans and White
segments.summary: He remembers Kid Punch, Kid Rene, Buddy Petit and Chris Kelly and Kid Punch playing on an open-air pavilion, and says their music was similar to today's.

segments.title: Buying a five-dollar Albert clarinet and first lessons with Chaligny
segments.summary: In 1923 he bought a B-flat Albert clarinet with his five-dollar Christmas savings, taught himself hymns, then took lessons from Old Man Chaligny.

segments.title: Chaligny's method book and his brass band
segments.summary: Chaligny taught from a real music book, recommended a clarinet book, and had a brass band that rehearsed at the Scent of Sinners club.

segments.title: Wellington Knox and the other clarinet students
segments.summary: His uncle Wellington Knox played in the band; they discuss whether he is related to Emile Knox of the Young Tuxedo band, and boys who gave up lessons.

segments.title: Lesson price, a strict teacher, and reading the red book
segments.summary: Lessons cost 25 cents for half an hour weekly; Chaligny slapped wrong notes, played only a poor trumpet, but taught him to read from a red brass band book for about a year.

segments.title: The Albert clarinet, John Lewis's loan, and Gerald Kendrick's band
segments.summary: He kept the 15-key Albert, borrowed a silver clarinet from John Lewis, rehearsed with Gilbert Young, then joined trumpeter Gerald Kendrick's band that played by ear.

segments.title: Kendrick's band members and losing the habit of reading
segments.summary: He can't name the trombonist in Kendrick's band, says playing by ear made him lose his reading, and is brushing up for a rehearsing band.

segments.title: Jobbing with Jack Carey, Kid Rene, Chris Kelly and Kid Thomas
segments.summary: After Kendrick he played a four-dollar job with Jack Carey, then with Kid Rene, Chris Kelly at the halls, and Kid Thomas's band across the river.

segments.title: Chris Kelly, Punch and Buddy Petit's playing; learning from records
segments.summary: He praises Chris Kelly's blues and plunger mute, Punch's trumpet variations and Buddy Petit and Kid Rene, and says he learned clarinet parts from Armstrong and Fazola records.

segments.title: How he got the nickname Cornbread
segments.summary: He was called Brother, and Cornbread from the school cornbread his mother packed; Brother William came from his father's name.

segments.title: The H&J Tavern and Russell first hearing him
segments.summary: Thomas switched to Boehm clarinet while at the H&J Tavern in World War II; Russell recalls hearing him there in 1943 on George Lewis's advice.

segments.title: Switching from Albert to Boehm system clarinet
segments.summary: He bought a Boehm clarinet for his son, who lost interest, so Thomas taught himself the fingering and now can't play the Albert.

segments.title: Tone, stiff reeds and playing without teeth
segments.summary: He finds a bigger tone on the Boehm, uses a stiff reed and a strong lip, and has long played without teeth, struggling to play with dentures.

segments.title: Mouthpiece and blowing softer on the Boehm
segments.summary: He used the mouthpiece that came with the Boehm clarinet and found he must blow softer or it squeaks; he returned George Lewis's silver Albert.

segments.title: The clarinets he has owned; wanting a Selmer
segments.summary: He has owned six or seven clarinets since his first, plays two Boehm clarinets, bought one from Peterson, and wants a Selmer.

segments.title: Saxophone worries, Leblanc and a horn bought via Larry Barbarin
segments.summary: He fears sax would hurt his clarinet lip, is told about Leblanc clarinets, and recalls buying a French clarinet through Larry Barbarin.

segments.title: Georgie Boyd as favorite clarinetist; his widow and photograph
segments.summary: His favorite young clarinetist was Georgie Boyd, whose widow gave Thomas his clarinet; Russell and Collins discuss locating her and a World War I photograph.

segments.title: Rubber bands on clarinets; giving an Albert to Handy
segments.summary: They discuss clarinetists who held keys with rubber bands, and Thomas gave his last Albert to Handy while recalling John Lewis and Piku trying Boehm.

segments.title: Zeb and George Boyd, friendship and death
segments.summary: He recalls the clarinetist Zeb and his friendship with George Boyd, who helped him, when Boyd died in the 1930s, and Kid Howard's kidding.

segments.title: Kid Howard's health and praise for old trumpeters
segments.summary: Kid Howard is doing fine after a musicians' banquet, and Thomas praises Punch, Petit, Rene and says he didn't know Bunk Johnson well.

segments.title: Hearing Armstrong in Papa Celestin's band
segments.summary: Thomas never heard Oliver but heard Armstrong in Papa Celestin's brass band at the fairgrounds, where Celestin started the band with a two-by-four.

segments.title: Years in the Original Tuxedo band; Eisenhower performance
segments.summary: He has been with the Original Tuxedo band 12 or 13 years, including a command performance for Eisenhower and the Absinthe House film.

segments.title: Planned Europe and South America trips; work after Celestin's death
segments.summary: Plans to take the band to Europe and South America collapsed when Celestin died; work dropped and then recovered under Eddie Pearson.

segments.title: Playing for the Delta Line ship sailings
segments.summary: The band plays three to four on alternate Mondays for Delta Line departures; schedules, boat names and winter cold are discussed.

segments.title: Albert leads the band; traveling by station wagon or bus
segments.summary: Albert is manager and leader; upcoming jobs include the Fairgrounds and a Pensacola yacht club, and the band travels by station wagon or bus, sharing the driving.

segments.title: Jeanette and Norvin Kimball
segments.summary: Thomas identifies pianist Jeanette Kimball and her ex-husband Norvin, and says Celestin took Jeanette into the band as a girl, so they should be interviewed.

segments.chapter: Other bands: Royal Jazz, H&J, Rainbow Room
segments.title: The Original Royal Jazz Band under Joe Harris
segments.summary: Before Celestin he played with Joe Harris's Original Royal Jazz Band, which played Odd Fellows parades and fairground picnics and weddings four or five nights a week.

segments.chapter: Other bands: Royal Jazz, H&J, Rainbow Room
segments.title: Six or seven years at the H&J; Blue and Wendell Eugene
segments.summary: He stayed with bands a long time, spent six or seven years at the H&J with Jacques Pierre, Emma Barris and trumpeter Blue, whose place Wendell Eugene took.

segments.chapter: Other bands: Royal Jazz, H&J, Rainbow Room
segments.title: Leaving the H&J for the Rainbow Room; union dues trouble
segments.summary: Moran and Bigfoot Bill brought him to the Rainbow Room; Bigfoot Bill paid his half union fee, but union officials objected until his receipt was shown.

segments.chapter: Other bands: Royal Jazz, H&J, Rainbow Room
segments.title: Drummer Jules (Jack) Pierre
segments.summary: They talk about Jack Pierre, who drummed at the H&J, may have played with Clayton, and may have sold Russell a banjo.

segments.chapter: Other bands: Royal Jazz, H&J, Rainbow Room
segments.title: Playing with Sheik, Kid Howard and Andrew Jefferson
segments.summary: He played with Sheik in St. Bernard and Delacroix Island, Kid Howard at Grand Isle, and Andrew Jefferson, who still gives him parade work.

segments.chapter: Other bands: Royal Jazz, H&J, Rainbow Room
segments.title: Playing clarinet for hospital patients during appendix surgery
segments.summary: At Charity Hospital for an appendix operation he entertained staff and patients on the clarinet, years before joining Celestin.

segments.chapter: Other bands: Royal Jazz, H&J, Rainbow Room
segments.title: The clarinets he now owns
segments.summary: He now owns three Boehm clarinets: a Regent, a Noble bought from Peterson, and one in a Leblanc case.

segments.title: Celestin's early big brass band versus the later smaller band
segments.summary: When Thomas joined, Celestin led seven to ten pieces, unlike the earlier twenty-piece brass band that used the two-by-four.

segments.title: Sound of the old brass bands
segments.summary: Old brass bands had no saxes but many clarinets and alto horns; Thomas says the instruments blended, with strong trumpets drowning the softer ones.

segments.title: Brass band experience and parades with Kid Rene
segments.summary: He played in pickup brass bands, never regularly in the old bands, and doesn't recall playing brass band with Kid Rene.

segments.title: Advertising trucks: seating arrangement
segments.summary: With Kid Rene he played dance halls and advertising trucks, where the trombone sat at the tailgate, the clarinet near the cab and the bass at the rear.

segments.title: Bass hit by a tree branch; bridge accident; the Yo-Yo Boys
segments.summary: He tells of a bass player pulled off a truck by a tree, Frank Mills's bass wrecked on a Mississippi bridge, and the Yo-Yo Boys with Andrew Jefferson and Stagley.

segments.title: Last advertising truck, about 1952
segments.summary: The last advertising truck he played was for Peter Williams's picnic, around 1952-53; bands rarely do this now.

segments.title: Where to find Mardi Gras Indians
segments.summary: Thomas tells where and when to see Indians, at Claiborne and Johnson or Nero around 8 a.m., and that they sing with tambourines.

segments.title: His sister Noella and the church choir
segments.summary: His sister arrives; he mentions her voice in St. Peter Claver choir, and repeats that the family was musically inclined.

segments.title: Other instruments tried and drumming on a soapbox
segments.summary: He nearly bought a trombone, wishes he had learned piano, and had beaten a soapbox before buying the clarinet.

segments.title: Cane reeds, homemade trimming and caulk grease
segments.summary: He uses cane reeds, trims them with nickels, a cigarette and a razor blade, buys at Peterson, and learned about caulk grease.

segments.title: Reed strengths: Peterson on numbers, choosing a three and a half
segments.summary: Peterson explained reed numbering, Thomas settled on three and a half for tone, and rejects advice to drop to two and a half.

segments.title: Joining Celestin at the American Legion Hall; Paddock Lounge split
segments.summary: He started with Celestin at the American Legion Hall when Bill Matthews's group fell out with Papa, and later became regular clarinetist after Paul Barnes left.

segments.title: Celestin's big band in 1946 and his comeback
segments.summary: Thomas wasn't in the 1946 big band at the Pelican; Celestin gave up music, worked at a shipyard, broke his leg, then made a comeback.

segments.title: Closing remarks
segments.summary: Russell ends the reel and both thank each other.
